claim: Ascending neuromodulatory projections from the locus coeruleus (LC) affect cortical neural networks via the release of norepinephrine (NE).
source: Ascending neuromodulatory projections from the locus coeruleus (LC) affect cortical neural networks via the release of norepinephrine (NE).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in neuroscience supported by the broader scientific literature.

claim: In awake monkeys, LC activation is associated with changes in coordinated activity patterns in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC).
source: Here, we show that in awake monkeys, LC activation is associated with changes in coordinated activity patterns in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The relationships between LC activation and ACC coordinated activity patterns are largely independent of changes in firing rates of individual ACC neurons.
source: These relationships, which are largely independent of changes in firing rates of individual ACC neurons, depend on the type of LC activation
evidence: This is supported by data showing no reliable relationships between LC and ACC single-neuron firing rates (Figure 2).

claim: ACC pairwise correlations tend to be reduced when ongoing (baseline) LC activity increases.
source: ACC pairwise correlations tend to be reduced when ongoing (baseline) LC activity increases but enhanced when external events evoke transient LC responses.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figures 3-5.

claim: ACC pairwise correlations are enhanced when external events evoke transient LC responses.
source: ACC pairwise correlations tend to be reduced when ongoing (baseline) LC activity increases but enhanced when external events evoke transient LC responses.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figures 7-8.

claim: Both relationships between LC activation and ACC correlations covary with pupil changes that reflect LC activation and arousal.
source: Both relationships covary with pupil changes that reflect LC activation and arousal.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 5 and 8 showing relationships between pupil changes, LC activity, and ACC correlations.

claim: Changes in brain state are associated with different levels of arousal, attention, motivation, surprise, and other factors that can affect the activity patterns of large populations of cortical neurons.
source: Changes in brain state are associated with different levels of arousal, attention, motivation, surprise, and other factors that can affect the activity patterns of large populations of cortical neurons (McAdams and Maunsell, 1999; Purcell et al., 2012; Chang et al., 2012; Falkner et al., 2013; Downer et al., 2015; Ecker et al., 2016; Thiele et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Changes in cortical activity patterns are thought to result, in part, from the widespread release of neuromodulators.
source: These changes are thought to result, in part, from the widespread release of neuromodulators (Aoki et al., 1987; Devauges and Sara, 1990; Schultz et al., 1993; Dalley et al., 2001; Bouret and Sara, 2005; Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; McGaughy et al., 2008; Salamone et al., 2009; Pinto et al., 2013; Varazzani et al., 2015; Khani and Rainer, 2016; Minces et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Different neuromodulatory systems have different anatomical and physiological properties.
source: Different neuromodulatory systems have different anatomical and physiological properties (Kupfermann, 1979; Aoki et al., 1987; Xiang et al., 1998; Flores-Hernandez et al., 2000; Fernández-Pastor and Meana, 2002; Ding and Perkel, 2002; Salgado et al., 2011; Herrero et al., 2013; Sugihara et al., 2016; Doyle and Meeks, 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The ACC has strong reciprocal connectivity, both structural and functional, with the LC.
source: We targeted the ACC because it has strong reciprocal connectivity, both structural and functional, with the LC (Lewis et al., 1979; Morrison et al., 1979; Porrino and Goldman-Rakic, 1982; Jones and Olpe, 1984; Fernández-Pastor et al., 2005; Gompf et al., 2010; Chandler and Waterhouse, 2012; Chandler et al., 2013; Tervo et al., 2014; Köhler et al., 2016; De Gee et al., 2017; Koga et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: ACC neural activity can encode computations that underlie adaptive, goal-directed behaviors.
source: Moreover, ACC neural activity can encode computations that underlie adaptive, goal-directed behaviors, including those that are also associated with indirect measures of LC-linked arousal, such as changes in pupil size and the P300 component of the event-related potential (ERP; Shima and Tanji, 1998; Gehring and Willoughby, 2002; Holroyd and Coles, 2002; Critchley et al., 2005; Matsumoto et al., 2007; Hayden et al., 2011; Shenhav et al., 2013; Ebitz and Platt, 2015; Sarafyazd and Jazayeri, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: During passive fixation, LC neurons were weakly active, with no spikes measured on more than a third of all trials.
source: During passive fixation, LC neurons were weakly active, with no spikes measured on more than a third of all trials and otherwise a median (interquartile range [IQR]) firing rate of 1.8 [0.9–3.6] sp/s measured during 1.1 s of stable fixation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The median firing rate of LC neurons during stable fixation was 1.8 [0.9–3.6] sp/s.
source: During passive fixation, LC neurons were weakly active, with no spikes measured on more than a third of all trials and otherwise a median (interquartile range [IQR]) firing rate of 1.8 [0.9–3.6] sp/s measured during 1.1 s of stable fixation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The mean and variance of ACC spike counts increased steadily as a function of the duration of the counting window.
source: The mean and variance of ACC spike counts, along with their Fano factor (the ratio of variance over mean), increased steadily as a function of the duration of the counting window.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: The Fano factor of ACC spike counts increased steadily as a function of the duration of the counting window.
source: The mean and variance of ACC spike counts, along with their Fano factor (the ratio of variance over mean), increased steadily as a function of the duration of the counting window.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: The mean, variance, and Fano factor measured in the ACC were, on average, slightly higher for LCzero versus LCnon-zero trials, but these relationships were not statistically reliable.
source: These trends showed an apparent, small relationship with simultaneously measured LC spiking activity, such that the mean, variance, and Fano factor measured in the ACC were, on average, slightly higher for LCzero versus LCnon-zero trials (Figure 2B–D). However, these relationships were not statistically reliable when considering data from both monkeys combined together and only in one case (Figure 2G) when considering data separately for each monkey (sign-rank test for H0: median difference between LCzero and LCnon-zero conditions computed per ACC unit, or ANOVA test for an effect of LC firing rate group, p > 0.05 in all cases; Figure 2B–G).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Pairwise spike-count correlations (rsc) in ACC had median [IQR] values of 0.03 [–0.01 0.07] using 200 ms counting windows.
source: Specifically, pairwise spike-count correlations (rsc) in ACC had median [IQR] values of 0.03 [–0.01 0.07] using 200 ms counting windows and systematically increased and became more variable across pairs with larger counting windows up to 1 s (0.05 [–0.03 0.14]; ANOVA test for effect of window size, p = 0.0243).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: ACC spike-count correlations systematically increased and became more variable across pairs with larger counting windows up to 1 s (0.05 [–0.03 0.14]).
source: Specifically, pairwise spike-count correlations (rsc) in ACC had median [IQR] values of 0.03 [–0.01 0.07] using 200 ms counting windows and systematically increased and became more variable across pairs with larger counting windows up to 1 s (0.05 [–0.03 0.14]; ANOVA test for effect of window size, p = 0.0243).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis (ANOVA test, p = 0.0243).

claim: ACC spike-count correlations were largest when measured using relatively large time windows, for ACC pairs that exhibited relatively large, positive correlations independent of LC firing, and when the simultaneously recorded LC neuron was not active.
source: Specifically, the correlations were largest when (1) they were measured using relatively large time windows; (2) for ACC pairs that exhibited relatively large, positive correlations independent of LC firing; and (3) when the simultaneously recorded LC neuron was not active (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: ACC rsc values from the upper two terciles of LC-independent rsc values were reduced by up to ~50% when computed on trials with at least one or more LC spike versus trials with no LC spikes.
source: Under these conditions, ACC rsc values from the upper two terciles of LC-independent rsc values were reduced by up to ~50% when computed on trials with at least one or more LC spike versus trials with no LC spikes (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: The magnitude of reductions in ACC rsc was not related in a consistent manner to the magnitude of LCnon-zero activity.
source: The magnitude of these reductions was not related in a consistent manner to the magnitude of LCnon-zero activity (ANOVA test for group effect of LC firing rates > 0).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA test).

claim: LC-linked differences in ACC rsc values did not result simply from changes in ACC neuron firing rates because the two measures were unrelated.
source: Furthermore, these LC-linked differences in ACC rsc values did not result simply from changes in ACC neuron firing rates because the two measures were unrelated (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There was a weak but statistically reliable relationship between LC-linked changes in ACC rsc and changes in ACC Fano factor.
source: We found a weak but statistically reliable relationship between LC-linked changes in ACC rsc and changes in ACC Fano factor (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Spike-count correlations (rsc) from simultaneously measured pairs of LC neurons did not depend systematically on concurrently measured ACC activity.
source: In contrast, spike-count correlations (rsc) from simultaneously measured pairs of LC neurons did not depend systematically on concurrently measured ACC activity.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: ACC-independent LC rsc values were roughly similar to LC-independent ACC rsc values, increasing steadily and becoming more variable as a function of the counting-window size.
source: In general, ACC-independent LC rsc values were roughly similar to LC-independent ACC rsc values, increasing steadily and becoming more variable as a function of the counting-window size; for example, median [IQR] values were 0.02 [0 0.09] for 200 ms windows and 0.06 [–0.02 0.19] for 1 s windows.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Differences in single-unit LC activity were associated with differences in coordinated activity patterns of pairs of neurons in ACC, but differences in single-unit ACC activity were not associated with differences in coordinated activity patterns of pairs of neurons in LC.
source: Thus, differences in single-unit LC activity were associated with differences in coordinated activity patterns of pairs of neurons in ACC, but differences in single-unit ACC activity were not associated with differences in coordinated activity patterns of pairs of neurons in LC.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 4 and 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: During passive fixation, there is a quasi-periodic fluctuation of the pupil.
source: During passive fixation, there is a quasi-periodic fluctuation of the pupil (Lowenstein and Loewenfeld, 1969; Pong and Fuchs, 2000; Joshi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The timing of LC spiking was related to the phase of ongoing pupil fluctuations, such that LC spiking tended to be higher preceding dilation versus constriction.
source: Consistent with our previous findings (Joshi et al., 2016), the timing of LC spiking was related to the phase of these ongoing pupil fluctuations, such that LC spiking tended to be higher preceding dilation versus constriction.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and prior research (Joshi et al., 2016).

claim: LC spiking modulations showed a systematic precession with dilation phase that corresponded to a delay of ~270 ms from the maximum modulation of LC activity to the relevant pupil change.
source: These modulations showed a systematic precession with dilation phase that corresponded to a delay of ~270 ms from the maximum modulation of LC activity to the relevant pupil change (Figure 5A; median of intercepts from linear regression of per-time-bin peaks of individual LC PETHs; bootstrapped 95% confidence interval from regression for each LC neuron = [177–353 ms]; for examples of pupil cycles and measurement epochs, see Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Pairwise correlations in ACC varied systematically with the phase of ongoing fluctuations in pupil diameter.
source: Combined with our current findings that pairwise correlations in ACC tended to be smaller when LC is active during passive fixation, these results predicted that pairwise correlations in ACC should also vary systematically with the phase of ongoing fluctuations in pupil diameter. We found such a relationship between pupil phase and ACC rsc values.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A brief, loud sound played on randomly selected fixation trials can elicit a transient pupil dilation as well as transient responses from individual LC neurons.
source: We showed previously that a brief, loud sound played on randomly selected fixation trials ('beep trials') can elicit a transient pupil dilation as well as transient responses from individual LC neurons (Joshi et al., 2016; evoked responses from an example LC neuron are shown in Figure 6A, and the LC population average from three monkeys is shown in Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by prior research (Joshi et al., 2016) and data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: The beep stimulus elicited a consistent, albeit weaker, response in the ACC.
source: The beep stimulus also elicited a consistent, albeit weaker, response in the ACC (evoked responses from an example ACC neuron are shown in Figure 6D, and the ACC population average from two monkeys is shown in Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: The averaged ACC response to the beep included a slight excitation and then inhibition relative to baseline within 200 ms of stimulus presentation.
source: The averaged ACC response included a slight excitation and then inhibition relative to baseline within 200 ms of stimulus presentation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The startle events caused transient reductions in the trial-to-trial variability (measured as the Fano factor) of spiking activity of individual neurons in both LC and ACC, with a slightly more sustained effect in the ACC.
source: The startle events also caused transient reductions in the trial-to-trial variability (measured as the Fano factor) of spiking activity of individual neurons in both LC and ACC, with a slightly more sustained effect in the ACC (Figure 6C and F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C and F.

claim: The reduction in neuronal variability following the onset of a stimulus, also referred to as quenching, has been reported previously for neurons in a range of other cortical regions and for a range of task conditions.
source: This reduction in neuronal variability following the onset of a stimulus, also referred to as quenching, has been reported previously for neurons in a range of other cortical regions and for a range of task conditions (Churchland et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: There was no evidence that the startling sound caused systematic changes in ACC coordinated activity when measured independently of the LC response.
source: In the ACC, we found no evidence that the startling sound caused systematic changes in coordinated activity when measured independently of the LC response. Specifically, spike-count correlations were highly variable across ACC neuron pairs, with no statistically reliable, systematic differences when compared before versus after the beep (comparing ACC rsc before versus after beep for spikes measured in 1 s bins; Mann–Whitney U-test, p > 0.05 for both monkeys).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis (Mann–Whitney U-test, p > 0.05).

claim: LC neurons did not show a characteristic transient response on every presentation of a startle stimulus: the median fraction of trials with a response was 54% for monkey Sp and 43% for monkey Ci.
source: Specifically, LC neurons did not show a characteristic transient response on every presentation of a startle stimulus: the median fraction of trials with a response that included a transient increase and then decrease in spiking activity was 54% for monkey Sp and 43% for monkey Ci (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: ACC rsc tended to be larger after versus before the beep stimulus, but only for the subset of trials in which the beep also elicited the characteristic LC response.
source: ACC rsc tended to be larger after versus before the beep stimulus, but only for the subset of trials in which the beep also elicited the characteristic LC response (Figure 6A and B), for both monkeys (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 6A-B and 7A.

claim: Modulations of ACC pairwise correlations did not reflect simply transient differences in LC firing rates but rather specific differences between the presence and absence of the stimulus-evoked LC response.
source: These modulations did not reflect simply transient differences in LC firing rates but rather specific differences between the presence and absence of the stimulus-evoked LC response (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Modulations of ACC pairwise correlations did not reflect LC-driven differences in the stimulus-driven quenching of response variability in ACC, which was similar on trials with and without LC-evoked responses.
source: These modulations of ACC pairwise correlations also did not reflect LC-driven differences in the stimulus-driven quenching of response variability in ACC, which was similar on trials with and without LC-evoked responses (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The magnitude of beep-evoked LC responses is correlated positively with the size of the simultaneously evoked change in pupil diameter.
source: We showed previously that the magnitude of beep-evoked LC responses is correlated positively with the size of the simultaneously evoked change in pupil diameter (Joshi et al., 2016). We reproduced those results in our current data set (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by prior research (Joshi et al., 2016) and data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Beep-evoked changes in ACC rsc that required an LC-evoked response were larger on trials in which the evoked LC response was accompanied by a large versus small pupil dilation.
source: In general, the beep-evoked changes in ACC rsc that required an LC-evoked response were larger on trials in which the evoked LC response was accompanied by a large versus small pupil dilation (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The relationship between beep-evoked changes in ACC rsc and pupil responses was not evident when considering baseline, not evoked, pupil size.
source: These effects were not evident when considering baseline, not evoked, pupil size (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: LC firing rates increased after the fixation point turned on and before stable fixation was acquired.
source: For no-beep trials, LC firing rates increased after the fixation point turned on and before stable fixation was acquired (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The epoch before stable fixation included elevated ACC rsc (particularly when the simultaneously recorded LC neuron was not active) that preceded the elevation in LC firing.
source: This epoch also included elevated ACC rsc (particularly when the simultaneously recorded LC neuron was not active, consistent with the results shown in Figure 4) that preceded the elevation in LC firing (Figure 9B, gray lines).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Both LC firing and ACC rsc tended to stabilize after stable fixation was attained.
source: Both LC firing and ACC rsc tended to stabilize after stable fixation was attained.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9A-B.

claim: The beep caused a transient increase in ACC rsc, and this increase tended to occur more rapidly on trials with versus without a concomitant LC response.
source: In general, the beep caused a transient increase in ACC rsc, and this increase tended to occur more rapidly on trials with (Figure 9D, gold shaded area) versus without (Figure 9F, gold shaded area) a concomitant LC response (Mann–Whitney U-test, for H0: the linear rate of increase of ACC rsc in this period was larger when LC neuron did versus did not respond, p = 0.0297).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9D and F and statistical analysis (Mann–Whitney U-test, p = 0.0297).

claim: The LC transient response peaked at the beginning of the epoch in which the ACC rsc started to increase.
source: Note that the LC transient response (Figure 9C) peaked at the beginning of the epoch in which the ACC rsc started to increase, which is consistent with the idea that the LC-evoked response drives (or at least coincides with) a faster rate of ACC rsc increase (steeper slope in the gold region in Figure 9D compared with F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9C-D and F, and involves inference about temporal relationships.

claim: The evoked LC response was associated with a more reliable and larger increase in ACC rsc later in the trial (500–1000 ms after the beep).
source: The evoked LC response was also associated with a more reliable and larger increase in ACC rsc later in the trial (compare Figure 9D and F; Mann–Whitney U-test for H0: ACC rsc 500–1000 ms after the beep was the same on trials with versus without a beep-evoked LC response, p = 0.0350 for both monkeys' data pooled together)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9D and F and statistical analysis (Mann–Whitney U-test, p = 0.0350).

claim: ACC rsc did not anticipate whether or not the beep would evoke an LC response.
source: but was not associated with differences in ACC rsc in the time just before the beep (i.e., ACC rsc did not anticipate whether or not the beep would evoke an LC response; Mann–Whitney U-test for H0: ACC rsc –500–0 ms before the beep was the same on trials with versus without a beep-evoked LC response, p = 0.0693 for both monkeys' data pooled together).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis (Mann–Whitney U-test, p = 0.0693).

claim: The context dependence of LC-ACC effects implies that spontaneous versus sensory-evoked activation of the LC-NE system can have different effects on coordinated patterns of activity in cortical networks.
source: The context dependence of these effects implies that spontaneous versus sensory-evoked activation of the LC-NE system can have different effects on coordinated patterns of activity in cortical networks.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings showing different effects under different conditions.

claim: Different temporal patterns of NE release could mediate a range of synaptic effects via distinct NE receptor subtypes with different affinities and different spatial distributions in different parts of the brain.
source: In principle, different temporal patterns of NE release could mediate a range of synaptic effects via distinct NE receptor subtypes with different affinities and different spatial distributions in different parts of the brain (Aoki et al., 1987; Nicholas et al., 1993; Arnsten et al., 1998; Arnsten, 2000; Berridge et al., 2012; Berridge and Spencer, 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Synaptic effects of NE can influence both excitatory and inhibitory neurons as well as astrocytes, resulting in changes in network dynamics in thalamus, cortex, and elsewhere.
source: These synaptic effects can influence both excitatory and inhibitory neurons as well as astrocytes, resulting in changes in network dynamics in thalamus, cortex, and elsewhere (Segal and Bloom, 1976; Dillier et al., 1978; Waterhouse et al., 1980; McCormick and Prince, 1988; Wang and McCormick, 1993; McLean and Waterhouse, 1994; Fernández-Pastor and Meana, 2002; Salgado et al., 2011; Salgado et al., 2016; Paukert et al., 2014; Guan et al., 2015; Schiemann et al., 2015; Sherpa et al., 2016; Garcia-Junco-Clemente et al., 2019; Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Ohshima et al., 2017; Rodenkirch et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The study did not find similarly reliable relationships between the spiking activity of individual neurons measured simultaneously in LC and ACC.
source: In contrast to the relationships that we identified between LC activation and coordinated ACC activity patterns, we did not find similarly reliable relationships between the spiking activity of individual neurons measured simultaneously in each of the two brain regions.
evidence: This is supported by the lack of statistically significant findings in Figure 2.

claim: Changes in single-unit ACC responses were not related reliably to properties of the concurrently measured LC response.
source: However, these changes in single-unit ACC responses were not related reliably to properties of the concurrently measured LC response that we could measure and thus may involve mechanisms other than the LC-NE system.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of reliable relationships found in the data.

claim: An increase in correlations is considered a possible mechanism for connecting neural populations over a range of spatial and temporal scales.
source: For example, an increase in correlations is considered a possible mechanism for connecting neural populations over a range of spatial and temporal scales (Gray et al., 1989; Singer, 1999; Riehle et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: An increase in correlated variability can negatively impact the information coding capacity of a large neural population, particularly over longer integration windows.
source: However, an increase in correlations can also negatively impact the information coding capacity of a large neural population, particularly over longer integration windows (Zohary et al., 1994; Bair et al., 2001; Averbeck et al., 2006; Renart et al., 2010; but also see Nirenberg and Latham, 2003 Moreno-Bote et al., 2014, for alternative interpretations).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Global states such as arousal and attention can modulate cortical correlations.
source: Global states such as arousal and attention (traditionally linked with LC-NE and cholinergic systems, respectively) can modulate cortical correlations (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Mitchell et al., 2009; Herrero et al., 2013; Schmidt et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Event-driven transient activation of LC could help to synchronize populations of cortical neurons by shifting them to a more correlated state.
source: Event-driven transient activation of LC could help to synchronize populations of cortical neurons by shifting them to a more correlated state.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: During nonevoked, ongoing (event-independent) firing, the NE release could enhance information processing and signal-to-noise ratios by reducing cortical correlations.
source: Conversely, during nonevoked, ongoing (event-independent) firing, the NE release could enhance information processing and signal-to-noise ratios by reducing cortical correlations.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Neural recordings were conducted in three adult male rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta).
source: Three adult male rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) were used for this study (monkeys Oz, Ci, and Sp).
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the Materials and methods section.

claim: The study recorded neural activity from 84 single units in LC from monkey Sp and 84 single units from monkey Ci.
source: We analyzed neural activity from simultaneously measured sites in the LC (n = 84 single units, including 78 simultaneously recorded pairs from 35 sites in monkey Sp; 84/80/31 in monkey Ci)
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the data collected.

claim: The study recorded neural activity from 372 single units in ACC from monkey Sp and 275 single units from monkey Ci.
source: and ACC (372/4336/35 in monkey Sp; 275/2875/31 in monkey Ci)
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the data collected.

claim: Fixation trials were of variable length (1–5 s, uniformly distributed).
source: Briefly, fixation trials were of variable length (1–5 s, uniformly distributed).
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the Materials and methods section.

claim: On a subset of randomly chosen trials (~25%), after 1–1.5 s of fixation a sound (1 kHz, 0.5 s) was played over a speaker.
source: On a subset of randomly chosen trials (~25%), after 1–1.5 s of fixation a sound (1 kHz, 0.5 s) was played over a speaker in the experimental booth ('beep trials').
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the Materials and methods section.

claim: LC+ units had relatively long action potential waveforms, were sensitive to arousing external stimuli, and decreased firing when the monkey was drowsy.
source: LC+ units had relatively long action potential waveforms, were sensitive to arousing external stimuli (e.g., door knocking), and decreased firing when the monkey was drowsy (e.g., eyelids drooped; Aston-Jones et al., 1994; Bouret and Sara, 2004; Bouret and Richmond, 2009).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing how LC neurons were identified, supported by citations.

claim: Recording sites were verified using MRI and assessing the effects of systemic injection of clonidine on LC+ responses in monkeys Oz and Ci and by histology with electrolytic lesions and electrode-tract reconstruction in monkey Oz.
source: Sites were verified using MRI and assessing the effects of systemic injection of clonidine on LC+ responses in monkeys Oz and Ci and by histology with electrolytic lesions and electrode-tract reconstruction in monkey Oz (Kalwani et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing verification procedures, supported by a citation.

claim: For ACC recordings, the study targeted the dorsal bank of the anterior cingulate sulcus, ~4–6 mm below the cortical surface.
source: For ACC recordings, we targeted the dorsal bank of the anterior cingulate sulcus, ~4–6 mm below the cortical surface.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the Materials and methods section.

claim: Spiking activity was considered only during stable fixation, defined as a 1.1 s window that began 1 s after attaining fixation in which the monkey's gaze remained within a square window 0.2° per side centered on the fixation point.
source: For each recorded neuron, we considered spiking activity only during stable fixation, defined as a 1.1 s window that began 1 s after attaining fixation in which the monkey's gaze remained within a square window 0.2° per side centered on the fixation point.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the Materials and methods section.
